1.q: וַ⁠תִּשָּׂא֙ כָּל־הָ֣⁠עֵדָ֔ה וַֽ⁠יִּתְּנ֖וּ אֶת־קוֹלָ֑⁠ם וַ⁠יִּבְכּ֥וּ הָ⁠עָ֖ם בַּ⁠לַּ֥יְלָה הַ⁠הֽוּא
1.note: The clauses **And all the congregation lifted up, and they gave their voice** and **and the people wept** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [And all the congregation wept very loudly in that night]

Here, the author is speaking as if the voices of the people were objects that they could **lift up** and **give**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And all the congregation made loud noises] or [And all the congregation cried out]

In this verse, the word **voice** is singular in form, but it refers to all the Israelites as a group. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural form of “voice.” Alternate translation: [their voices]

2.q: לוּ־מַ֨תְנוּ֙ בְּ⁠אֶ֣רֶץ מִצְרַ֔יִם א֛וֹ בַּ⁠מִּדְבָּ֥ר הַ⁠זֶּ֖ה לוּ־מָֽתְנוּ
2.note: The Israelites are using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling, hopelessness and despair. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. If not, you could say what the Israelites were feeling, or you could say what made them sad. Alternate translation: [It would have been better for us to die in the land of Egypt! It would be better for us to die in this wilderness!]

2.q: לוּ־מַ֨תְנוּ֙ בְּ⁠אֶ֣רֶץ מִצְרַ֔יִם א֛וֹ בַּ⁠מִּדְבָּ֥ר הַ⁠זֶּ֖ה לוּ־מָֽתְנוּ
2.note: It might seem that the expression **if only we died** contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [If only we died in the land of Egypt or in this wilderness!]

By **we**, the Israelites mean to include themselves but not Moses and Aaron to whom they are speaking, so use the exclusive form of that word in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

3.q: וְ⁠לָ⁠מָ֣ה יְ֠הוָה מֵבִ֨יא אֹתָ֜⁠נוּ אֶל־הָ⁠אָ֤רֶץ הַ⁠זֹּאת֙ לִ⁠נְפֹּ֣ל בַּ⁠חֶ֔רֶב
3.note: The Israelites are using the question form to express their complaint against Yahweh. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [We do not like how Yahweh has brought us to this land, since we will fall by the sword.]

By **us … Our wives and our children … for us**, the Israelites mean themselves, their families, and others in the congregation, but excluding Moses and Aaron to whom they are speaking, so use the exclusive form of those words if your language marks that distinction.

The phrase **to fall by the sword** is a common expression of this culture that means “to die in battle.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to die in battle]

By **for plunder**, the Israelites mean that their families would be taken away as slaves. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [slaves]

The Israelites are using the question form to make a strong statement that they believe returning to Egypt would be good for them. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [It is good for us to return to Egypt.]

4.note: The phrase **a man to his brother** is a common expression of this culture that means “to one another.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And they said to one another]

Here, the Israelites are speaking of appointing a leader as if they would **give a head**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [We shall appoint a chief]

By **We**, the Israelites mean to include themselves and also the other Israelites to whom they are speaking, so use the inclusive form of that word in your language if your language marks that distinction.

5.note: **Falling on their faces** was a symbolic action by which Moses and Aaron showed their dismay and grief at the Israelites’ rebellion. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [And Moses lay and Aaron with their faces on the ground to show their grief] or [And Moses bowed and Aaron with their faces to the ground in sorrow]
If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about **Aaron** with the information about **Moses**. Alternate translation: [And Moses and Aaron fell]

Here, **to the face of** represents being in front of the Israelite assembly. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in the presence of]

The author is using the possessive form to describe an **assembly** that is made up of **the congregation** that is **the sons of Israel**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the congregation that consists of all the sons of Israel assembled together]

The terms **assembly** and **congregation** mean similar things. The author is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [the congregation]

6.note: The words **Nun** and **Jephunneh** are the names of men.

The phrase **from the ones exploring the land** is a common expression of this culture that means “who were among those who explored the land.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [who were among those who explored the land]

The act of tearing their clothes was a symbolic action by which Joshua and Caleb showed their extreme distress and grief over the people’s unbelief. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [tore their clothes in sorrow] or [were so distressed that they ripped their clothes]

7.note: Here, the word **saying** introduces a direct quotation. See how you translated **saying** in [1:1](ta:01).
By **we**, Joshua and Caleb mean themselves but not the other Israelites to whom they are speaking, so use the exclusive form of that word in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

The author is repeating forms of the word **very** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [an incredibly good land]

8.q: אִם־חָפֵ֥ץ בָּ֨⁠נוּ֙ יְהוָ֔ה וְ⁠הֵבִ֤יא אֹתָ֨⁠נוּ֙ אֶל־הָ⁠אָ֣רֶץ הַ⁠זֹּ֔את
8.note: The author is describing a possible condition in which **he will bring us to this land** will take place only if **Yahweh delights in us** occurs first. Express this possible condition in a way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Suppose that Yahweh delights in us. In that case, he will bring us to this land]
By **us**, Joshua and Caleb mean to include both themselves and their Israelite listeners, so use the inclusive form of that word if your language marks that distinction.

Here, Joshua and Caleb are speaking of Canaan as if it were a land that had streams of **milk and honey** flowing through it. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated this clause in 13:27. Alternate translation: [is rich and fertile] or [is very productive]

9.note: Here the word **Only** introduces something that is very important because of the previous statement. If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [So it is important that]

9.q: וְ⁠אַתֶּ֗ם אַל־תִּֽירְאוּ֙ אֶת־עַ֣ם הָ⁠אָ֔רֶץ כִּ֥י לַחְמֵ֖⁠נוּ הֵ֑ם
9.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that **you shall not fear the people of the land** describes. Alternate translation: [and because the people of the land are our bread, you, you shall not fear them]

Here the author is repeating the pronoun **you** along with the verb translated as **shall not fear**, which already includes its meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that the Israelites should trust God rather than be afraid. If a speaker of your language would use explicit pronouns for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing that meaning here. Alternate translation: [and you shall not fear]

Here, Joshua and Caleb are speaking as if the Canaanites were actually **bread**. They mean that the Israelites will defeat them as easily as they eat food. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they are like our bread] or [we will conquer them as easily as eating bread]

Here, Joshua and Caleb are speaking as if the protection the Canaanites had were actually a **shadow** that had departed from them. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Any protection they had is gone]

10.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this as a direct quotation. Alternate translation: [And all the congregation said, “Stone them with stones!”]

It might seem that the expression **to stone them with stones** contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [to stone them]
Here, the pronoun **them** could refer to: (1) Caleb and Joshua. Alternate translation: [them, that is, Caleb and Joshua,] (2) Moses and Aaron. Alternate translation: [Moses and Aaron]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **glory**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [But Yahweh showed himself gloriously]

Here, the author could mean that Yahweh’s glory appeared: (1) at or near **the tent of meeting**. Alternate translation: [near the tent of meeting] (2) inside **the tent of meeting**. Alternate translation: [inside the tent of meeting]

11.q: עַד־אָ֥נָה יְנַאֲצֻ֖⁠נִי הָ⁠עָ֣ם הַ⁠זֶּ֑ה וְ⁠עַד־אָ֨נָה֙ לֹא־יַאֲמִ֣ינוּ בִ֔⁠י בְּ⁠כֹל֙ הָֽ⁠אֹת֔וֹת אֲשֶׁ֥ר עָשִׂ֖יתִי בְּ⁠קִרְבּֽ⁠וֹ
11.note: Yahweh is using the question form to express his anger and frustration that the people keep rejecting him and not believing in him. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate these questions as statements or as exclamations. Alternate translation: [This people needs to stop spurning me! And they need to stop not believing in me, in all the signs that I have done in its midst!]

The pronoun **it** refers to the people of Israel, and the pronoun **its** refers to the same group. In Hebrew, these pronouns are singular, even though they refer to a group of people. If it would be more natural in your language, you could use plural pronouns as in the alternate translation. Alternate translation: [will this people not believe … in their midst]

12.note: The pronoun **it** refers to the Israelite people. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [I will strike this people … and I will dispossess them … than they]

The implication is that Yahweh will kill the people with a plague. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. See the discussion of the term “struck” in the Introduction to Numbers. Alternate translation: [I will make it die]

Yahweh is not referring to a specific **plague**. He means an unspecified plague. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [with a plague]

By **I will make you into a nation**, Yahweh means he will make Moses’ descendants into a nation. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and I will make your offspring into a nation]

13.note: If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [But Egypt shall hear] or [Then Egypt shall hear]

By **Egypt shall hear**, Moses means that the Egyptians will hear about what Yahweh has done to the Israelites. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [And Egypt shall hear if you do those things]
Here, **Egypt** represents the people of Egypt. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the people of Egypt]

The word translated as **for** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. In this case, the Egyptians will hear because they are the ones from whom God rescued the Israelites. Alternate translation: [for they are paying attention because you brought this people up]

In keeping with what is usual for his language and culture, Moses is marking travel for change in elevation. If the expression **you brought this people up** contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [you brought this people]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **power**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in a powerful way]

14.note: The implication is that they will tell others about what Yahweh had done to Israel. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and they shall tell what you did]

In this verse, the word **one dwelling** is singular in form, but it refers to all inhabitants of Canaan as a group. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural form of “one dwelling.” Alternate translation: [to the ones dwelling]

Moses is using the expression **eye in eye** as a common expression of his culture to mean “face to face” or “directly.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [who appears face to face, you, Yahweh] or [who appears so that they can see you plainly, Yahweh]

Here Moses is speaking of the **cloud** as if it were a living thing that could stand over people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the similar figures of speech in Numbers 9:17–19. Alternate translation: [and you have your cloud hover over them]

Moses is using the possessive form to describe a **cloud** that looks like a **pillar** and **fire** that looks like a **pillar**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and in a cloud in the shape of a pillar … and in fire in the shape of a pillar]

Here, Moses is speaking of Yahweh as if he were **going before** the people to show them the way. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you are guiding]

Here, **to their face** represents being in front of the people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [before them]

15.q: לֵ⁠אמֹֽר׃ מִ⁠בִּלְתִּ֞י יְכֹ֣לֶת יְהוָ֗ה לְ⁠הָבִיא֙ אֶת־הָ⁠עָ֣ם הַ⁠זֶּ֔ה אֶל־הָ⁠אָ֖רֶץ אֲשֶׁר־נִשְׁבַּ֣ע לָ⁠הֶ֑ם וַ⁠יִּשְׁחָטֵ֖⁠ם בַּ⁠מִּדְבָּֽר
15.note: The phrase **day and night** is a common way of expressing “all the time” in biblical languages. Moses is expressing that the Israelites should meditate on the law continuously. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use an expression that means “all the time” or “continually.” Alternate translation: [saying that from Yahweh not being able to bring this people to the land that he swore to them, so he slaughtered them in the wilderness.]

The word **And** introduces the “if” portion of a hypothetical statement. Moses is describing a possible condition in which the nations saying certain things will take place only if Yahweh kills all the Israelites. Express this possible condition in a way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [If you kill]

The point of this comparison is that just as killing **one man** is quick and complete, so would be killing all the Israelites at once. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [at one time] or [as quickly as killing one man]

Moses is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [heard about you]

16.q: מִ⁠בִּלְתִּ֞י יְכֹ֣לֶת יְהוָ֗ה לְ⁠הָבִיא֙ אֶת־הָ⁠עָ֣ם הַ⁠זֶּ֔ה אֶל־הָ⁠אָ֖רֶץ אֲשֶׁר־נִשְׁבַּ֣ע לָ⁠הֶ֑ם וַ⁠יִּשְׁחָטֵ֖⁠ם בַּ⁠מִּדְבָּֽר
16.note: The word translated as **From** indicates that what follows is a reason for what comes after. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what comes after. Alternate translation: [‘Because Yahweh was not able to bring this people to the land that he swore to them, he slaughtered them in the wilderness’]

Moses is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [that he swore to hand over to them]

17.q: לֵ⁠אמֹֽר & אֶ֤רֶךְ אַפַּ֨יִם֙ וְ⁠רַב־חֶ֔סֶד נֹשֵׂ֥א עָוֺ֖ן וָ⁠פָ֑שַׁע וְ⁠נַקֵּה֙ לֹ֣א יְנַקֶּ֔ה פֹּקֵ֞ד עֲוֺ֤ן אָבוֹת֙ עַל־בָּנִ֔ים עַל־שִׁלֵּשִׁ֖ים וְ⁠עַל־רִבֵּעִֽים
17.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [saying that Yahweh is long of nostrils and great of covenant faithfulness, lifting up iniquity and transgression, and that leaving unpunished, he will not leave unpunished, counting iniquity of fathers upon sons, upon thirds, and upon fourths.]

If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [Therefore]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **power**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [may my Lord act very powerfully]

Even though Moses is addressing Yahweh directly, he is speaking of him in the third person as **my Lord** to show respect. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in a respectful form in the second person. Alternate translation: [of you, my Lord,]

18.note: Yahweh is speaking of himself in the third person as **Yahweh**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [I, Yahweh, am … I will not leave unpunished]

The phrase **long of nostrils** is a common expression of this culture that means “slow to anger” or “patient.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [slow to anger] or [patient]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and completely faithful to his promises]

Here, Yahweh is speaking of forgiving sins as if a person were **lifting up** a heavy object and taking it away. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [granting forgiveness for]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **iniquity** and **transgression**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [what people do that is evil and that breaks my laws]

Yahweh is repeating forms of the verb **leave unpunished** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [But he will definitely not leave unpunished]

Here, Yahweh could be implying that he **will not leave unpunished**: (1) a different group of people than the ones he forgives. Alternate translation: [he will not leave other people unpunished] (2) the same group of people he forgives, who will receive some punishment despite being forgiven. Alternate translation: [he will not leave them completely unpunished]

18.q: פֹּקֵ֞ד עֲוֺ֤ן אָבוֹת֙ עַל־בָּנִ֔ים עַל־שִׁלֵּשִׁ֖ים וְ⁠עַל־רִבֵּעִֽים
18.note: Here, Yahweh is speaking of passing down the consequences of sin as if it were **visiting iniquity** upon later generations. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [making iniquity of fathers apply to sons, to thirds, and to fourths]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **iniquity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what fathers did that was evil]

Here, **iniquity** represents the punishment for wrongdoing. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the punishment for iniquity]

Yahweh assumes that readers will know that **thirds** and **fourths** refer to the third and fourth generations of descendants. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [upon the people of the third generation, and upon the people of the fourth generation]

19.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **iniquity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [for what they did that was evil]

If your language does not use an abstract nouns for the ideas of **greatness** and **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [according to how much you are completely faithful to your promises]

Here, Moses is speaking of forgiveness as if it were “lifting up.” You may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the similar phrase in 14:18. Alternate translation: [you granted forgiveness]

Moses is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [for this people as they came from Egypt to this place]

20.note: Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [I have forgiven their iniquity]

Yahweh is using the term **word** to represent what Moses said by using words. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [according to your request]

21.q: וְ⁠אוּלָ֖ם חַי־אָ֑נִי וְ⁠יִמָּלֵ֥א כְבוֹד־יְהוָ֖ה אֶת־כָּל־הָ⁠אָֽרֶץ׃ כִּ֣י כָל־הָ⁠אֲנָשִׁ֗ים הָ⁠רֹאִ֤ים אֶת־כְּבֹדִ⁠י֙
21.note: Here, the phrase **all the land is filled with the glory of Yahweh** could be: (1) a second thing that Yahweh swears by. In this case, the phrase **that all the men** introduces what Yahweh swears. Alternate translation: [However, just as I live and just as all the land is filled with the glory of Yahweh, so all the men seeing my glory] (2) what Yahweh swears. In this case, the phrase **that all the men** introduces the reason for what Yahweh says in 14:23. Alternate translation: [However, as I live, so all the land shall be filled with the glory of Yahweh. Because all the men saw my glory]

Following the custom of this culture, Yahweh is swearing an oath and guaranteeing it by his own life and by how **all the land is filled with the glory of Yahweh**. Alternate translation: [I swear by my life and by how all the land is filled with the glory of Yahweh]

The expression **is filled** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is God. Alternate translation: [as I fill all the land]
Yahweh is speaking of himself in the third person as **Yahweh**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [with my glory]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **glory**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [with my glorious presence]

22.note: Here the masculine term **men** has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [the men and women]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **glory**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how glorious I am]

Here, the phrase **ten times** could refer to: (1) many times, with **ten** standing for a significant number of **times**. Alternate translation: [these many times] (2) **ten** specific **times**. Alternate translation: [these ten individual times]
The pronoun **this** refers to the **ten times** when the Israelites tested God. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [these]
Here, **my voice** represents what Yahweh told them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [what I told them]

23.note: Following the custom of this culture, Yahweh is swearing an oath by stating the first part of a condition (**if they see the land that I swore to their fathers**) but not the second part (“then”). If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explicitly state the second part of this condition. Alternate translation: [if they see the land that I swore to their fathers, may I strike myself dead]

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. See how you translated the similar clause in verse 16. Alternate translation: [that I swore to hand over to their fathers]
Yahweh is using the term **fathers** to mean “ancestors.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to their predecessors]

Here the word **And** introduces a restatement that affirms the oath. If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [In the end, all]

Here, Yahweh is speaking of seeing the land to mean entering and experiencing it personally. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [will not enter it] or [will not live in it]

24.note: Here, Yahweh is speaking of Caleb’s attitude and character as if it were a **spirit** that was with him. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [because he had a different attitude]

Here, Yahweh is speaking of Caleb’s faithfulness as if it were physically filling up the space behind Yahweh. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he was fully obedient to me] or [he was completely loyal to me]
In a context such as this, your language might say “take” instead of **bring**. Alternate translation: [so I will take him]

Here, Yahweh is speaking of Caleb’s descendants as if they were actually his **seed**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and his offspring]

25.note: The sentence **And the Amalekite and the Canaanite are dwelling in the valley** could be: (1) a reason why the Israelites must go back to the wilderness. Alternate translation: [Now here is why you travel as I command: the Amalekite and the Canaanite are dwelling in the valley.] (2) a description of the area that Caleb’s offspring will inherit. Alternate translation: [His seed will possess a valley where the Amalekite and the Canaanite are dwelling] (3) an explanation that the author has included inside the quote. Alternate translation: [(It is important to know that the Amalekite and the Canaanite are dwelling in the valley.)]

Here, **the Amalekite** and **the Canaanite** represent Amalekites and Canaanites in general, not specific individuals. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use expressions that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And the Amalekites and the Canaanites]
Here, the phrase **the valley** could refer to: (1) a specific, nearby valley. Alternate translation: [in the valley near here] (2) many valleys in the region. Alternate translation: [in the valleys]
The word **you** is plural here because Yahweh is addressing the Israelites, so use the plural form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.
It might seem that the expression **for you** contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [and set out]

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe a **way** that leads to **the Sea of Reeds**. This may refer to a well-known road. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the way that leads to the Sea of Reeds]

27.q: עַד־מָתַ֗י לָ⁠עֵדָ֤ה הָֽ⁠רָעָה֙ הַ⁠זֹּ֔את אֲשֶׁ֛ר הֵ֥מָּה מַלִּינִ֖ים עָלָ֑⁠י אֶת־תְּלֻנּ֞וֹת בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֗ל אֲשֶׁ֨ר הֵ֧מָּה מַלִּינִ֛ים עָלַ֖⁠י שָׁמָֽעְתִּי
27.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about Yahweh hearing the complaints of the Israelites before his question about how long he must endure **this evil congregation, that they are murmuring against me**. Alternate translation: [I have heard the murmurings of the sons of Israel, which they are murmuring against me. Until when to this evil congregation, that they are murmuring against me?]

27.q: עַד־מָתַ֗י לָ⁠עֵדָ֤ה הָֽ⁠רָעָה֙ הַ⁠זֹּ֔את אֲשֶׁ֛ר הֵ֥מָּה מַלִּינִ֖ים עָלָ֑⁠י
27.note: Yahweh is using the question form to express his frustration with the Israelites’ constant complaining. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [This evil congregation needs to stop murmuring against me!]

27.q: עַד־מָתַ֗י לָ⁠עֵדָ֤ה הָֽ⁠רָעָה֙ הַ⁠זֹּ֔את אֲשֶׁ֛ר הֵ֥מָּה מַלִּינִ֖ים
27.note: Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [Until when will this evil congregation escape punishment, for they are murmuring]

27.q: אֶת־תְּלֻנּ֞וֹת בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֗ל אֲשֶׁ֨ר הֵ֧מָּה מַלִּינִ֛ים עָלַ֖⁠י
27.note: The term **murmurings** and the phrase **they are murmuring** come from the same root word. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [what the sons of Israel are murmuring against me]

28.q: אֱמֹ֣ר אֲלֵ⁠הֶ֗ם חַי־אָ֨נִי֙ נְאֻם־יְהוָ֔ה אִם־לֹ֕א כַּ⁠אֲשֶׁ֥ר דִּבַּרְתֶּ֖ם בְּ⁠אָזְנָ֑⁠י כֵּ֖ן אֶֽעֱשֶׂ֥ה לָ⁠כֶֽם
28.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Say to them that as I live—the declaration of Yahweh—if not just as they spoke in my ears, thus I will do to them]
The word **Say** is singular here because Yahweh is speaking only to Moses. So use the singular form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

Following the custom of this culture, Yahweh is swearing an oath and guaranteeing it by something that he holds sacred: his life. For another example of this kind of oath, see verse 21. Alternate translation: [I swear by my life]

If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put **the declaration of Yahweh** before the oath rather than interrupting the oath. Alternate translation: [This is the declaration of Yahweh: As I live, if not]

28.q: אִם־לֹ֕א כַּ⁠אֲשֶׁ֥ר דִּבַּרְתֶּ֖ם בְּ⁠אָזְנָ֑⁠י כֵּ֖ן אֶֽעֱשֶׂ֥ה לָ⁠כֶֽם
28.note: Following the custom of this culture, Yahweh is swearing an oath by stating the first part of a condition (**if not just as you spoke in my ears, thus I will do to you**) but not the second part (“then”). If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explicitly state the second part of this condition. Alternate translation: [if I do not do to you exactly what you spoke in my ears, may I strike myself dead]

Yahweh is using the term **in my ears** to mean hearing. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the similar phrase in [11:1](ta:11). Alternate translation: [while I could hear]

29.q: בַּ⁠מִּדְבָּ֣ר הַ֠⁠זֶּה יִפְּל֨וּ פִגְרֵי⁠כֶ֜ם וְ⁠כָל־פְּקֻדֵי⁠כֶם֙ לְ⁠כָל־מִסְפַּרְ⁠כֶ֔ם מִ⁠בֶּ֛ן עֶשְׂרִ֥ים שָׁנָ֖ה וָ⁠מָ֑עְלָ⁠ה אֲשֶׁ֥ר הֲלִֽינֹתֶ֖ם עָלָֽ⁠י
29.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [In this wilderness their corpses will fall and all their counted ones according to all their number, from a son of 20 years and upward, who murmured against me]

Yahweh is using **your corpses will fall** as a common expression of this culture to mean “you will die.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you will experience death]

Here the word **and** introduces an explanation. If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [will fall, that is, all]

The expression **counted ones** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is the Israelite leaders. See how you translated the similar phrase in 2:4. Alternate translation: [and all of you whom your leaders counted]

The phrase **from a son of 20 years and upward** is a common expression of this culture that means “those who were 20 years old or older.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated this phrase in 1:3. Alternate translation: [those who were 20 years old or older]

30.q: אִם־אַתֶּם֙ תָּבֹ֣אוּ אֶל־הָ⁠אָ֔רֶץ אֲשֶׁ֤ר נָשָׂ֨אתִי֙ אֶת־יָדִ֔⁠י לְ⁠שַׁכֵּ֥ן אֶתְ⁠כֶ֖ם בָּ֑⁠הּ כִּ֚י אִם־כָּלֵ֣ב בֶּן־יְפֻנֶּ֔ה וִ⁠יהוֹשֻׁ֖עַ בִּן־נֽוּן׃ וְ⁠טַ֨פְּ⁠כֶ֔ם אֲשֶׁ֥ר אֲמַרְתֶּ֖ם לָ⁠בַ֣ז יִהְיֶ֑ה
30.note: If, in your language, it would appear that Yahweh was making a statement here and then contradicting it, you could reverse the order of the clauses so that the exception is stated first and then the larger group is named second. If you do, you may need to combine 14:30 and 14:31. Alternate translation: [except for Caleb, the son of Jephunneh, and Joshua, the son of Nun, and your children whom you said will be for plunder, if you go to the land that I have lifted up my hand to make you dwell in it]

30.q: אִם־אַתֶּם֙ תָּבֹ֣אוּ אֶל־הָ⁠אָ֔רֶץ אֲשֶׁ֤ר נָשָׂ֨אתִי֙ אֶת־יָדִ֔⁠י לְ⁠שַׁכֵּ֥ן אֶתְ⁠כֶ֖ם בָּ֑⁠הּ כִּ֚י אִם־כָּלֵ֣ב בֶּן־יְפֻנֶּ֔ה וִ⁠יהוֹשֻׁ֖עַ בִּן־נֽוּן
30.note: If you decided in the previous verse to translate this quotation in such a way that there would not be a quotation within a quotation, you can continue doing that here. Alternate translation: [if they go to the land that I have lifted up my hand to make them dwell in it, except Caleb, the son of Jephunneh, and Joshua, the son of Nun]

30.q: אִם־אַתֶּם֙ תָּבֹ֣אוּ אֶל־הָ⁠אָ֔רֶץ אֲשֶׁ֤ר נָשָׂ֨אתִי֙ אֶת־יָדִ֔⁠י לְ⁠שַׁכֵּ֥ן אֶתְ⁠כֶ֖ם בָּ֑⁠הּ
30.note: Following the custom of this culture, Yahweh is swearing an oath by stating the first part of a condition (**if you go to the land that I have lifted up my hand to make you dwell in it**) but not the second part (“then”). If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explicitly state the second part of this condition. Alternate translation: [may I strike myself dead if you go to the land that I have lifted up my hand to make you dwell in it]

The expression **lifted up my hand** was a symbolic action by which Yahweh showed that he was making a solemn oath or promise. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [I have sworn by lifting up my hand]

31.q: וְ⁠טַ֨פְּ⁠כֶ֔ם אֲשֶׁ֥ר אֲמַרְתֶּ֖ם לָ⁠בַ֣ז יִהְיֶ֑ה וְ⁠הֵבֵיאתִ֣י אֹתָ֔⁠ם וְ⁠יָֽדְעוּ֙ אֶת־הָ⁠אָ֔רֶץ אֲשֶׁ֥ר מְאַסְתֶּ֖ם בָּֽ⁠הּ
31.note: If you decided in the previous verse to translate this quotation in such a way that there would not be a quotation within a quotation, you can continue doing that here. Alternate translation: [and their children whom they said will be for plunder. And I will bring those children, and they will know the land that their parents rejected]

The implication is that some people had said the Israelite children would be taken as plunder or slaves by the Canaanites. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. See how you translated the similar phrase in verse 3. Alternate translation: [slaves]
If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this as a direct quotation. Alternate translation: [about whom you said, “They will be for plunder.”]

By **I will bring them**, Yahweh means he will bring them to the land of Canaan. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [And I will bring them to Canaan]
In a context such as this, your language might say “take” instead of **bring**. Alternate translation: [And I will take them]

Here, **know** represents experiencing and being familiar with the land. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and they will live in] or [and they will enjoy]

32.note: If you decided in the previous verse to translate this quotation in such a way that there would not be a quotation within a quotation, you can continue doing that here. Alternate translation: [And they, their corpses will fall in this wilderness]

Yahweh is stating the pronoun **you** separately, even though the phrase translated as **your corpses** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to transition clearly from speaking about the children of the Israelites to the Israelites themselves. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [But concerning you, your corpses]

Yahweh is using **your corpses will fall** as a common expression of this culture to mean “you will die.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated this phrase in verse 29. Alternate translation: [And you, you will experience death]

33.q: וּ֠⁠בְנֵי⁠כֶם יִהְי֨וּ רֹעִ֤ים בַּ⁠מִּדְבָּר֙ אַרְבָּעִ֣ים שָׁנָ֔ה וְ⁠נָשְׂא֖וּ אֶת־זְנוּתֵי⁠כֶ֑ם עַד־תֹּ֥ם פִּגְרֵי⁠כֶ֖ם בַּ⁠מִּדְבָּֽר
33.note: If you decided in the previous verse to translate this quotation in such a way that there would not be a quotation within a quotation, you can continue doing that here. Alternate translation: [and their sons will be shepherds in the wilderness 40 years, and their sons will lift up their fornications until the finishing of their corpses in the wilderness]

Here the masculine term **sons** has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [and your sons and daughters]

The implication is that the sons will wander from place to place in the wilderness as they care for their flocks. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [will be shepherds who roam]

Here, Yahweh is speaking of the Israelites’ unfaithfulness to him as if it were sexual unfaithfulness (**fornications**). Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your faithlessness]

Here, Yahweh is speaking of the Israelites’ **fornications** as if they were a burden that their children would carry. This refers to the consequences of their unfaithfulness to Yahweh that their children would experience. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and they will be punished for your fornications] or [they will bear the penalty of your fornications]

The phrase **until the finishing of your corpses** is a common expression of this culture that means “until the last one of you has died.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [until the last one of you experiences death]

34.q: בְּ⁠מִסְפַּ֨ר הַ⁠יָּמִ֜ים אֲשֶׁר־תַּרְתֶּ֣ם אֶת־הָ⁠אָרֶץ֮ אַרְבָּעִ֣ים יוֹם֒ י֣וֹם לַ⁠שָּׁנָ֞ה י֣וֹם לַ⁠שָּׁנָ֗ה תִּשְׂאוּ֙ אֶת־עֲוֺנֹ֣תֵי⁠כֶ֔ם אַרְבָּעִ֖ים שָׁנָ֑ה וִֽ⁠ידַעְתֶּ֖ם אֶת־תְּנוּאָתִֽ⁠י
34.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [By the number of the days that they explored the land, 40 days, a day for the year, a day for the year, they will lift up their iniquities 40 years. And they will know my opposition.]

Yahweh is using the common expression of this culture **a day for the year, a day for the year** to mean “one year for each day.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [one day to one year] or [one year for each day]

Here, Yahweh is speaking as if **iniquities** were a physical burden that the Israelites could lift up. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the similar clause in verse 33. Alternate translation: [you will be punished for your iniquities] or [you will bear the penalty of your iniquities]
If your language does not use abstract nouns for the idea of **iniquities**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what you did that was evil]

Here, the word translated **opposition** could refer to: (1) enmity. Alternate translation: [my enmity] (2) displeasure. Alternate translation: [my displeasure] (3) absence. Alternate translation: [my absence]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **opposition**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what it is like for me to oppose you]

35.note: The implication is that when Yahweh speaks something, it will certainly happen. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [I, Yahweh, have spoken, so it will happen]

35.q: אִם־לֹ֣א ׀ זֹ֣את אֶֽעֱשֶׂ֗ה לְ⁠כָל־הָ⁠עֵדָ֤ה הָֽ⁠רָעָה֙ הַ⁠זֹּ֔את הַ⁠נּוֹעָדִ֖ים עָלָ֑⁠י
35.note: Following the custom of this culture, Yahweh is swearing an oath by stating the first part of a condition (**if I do not do this to all this evil congregation, the ones congregating against me**) but not the second part (“then”). If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explicitly state the second part of this condition. Alternate translation: [If I do not do this to all this evil congregation, the ones congregating against me, may I strike myself dead]

Here, the pronoun **this** could refer to: (1) what Yahweh has declared in the previous verses. Alternate translation: [those things] (2) what he says at the end of this verse. Alternate translation: [what I am about to say]

These two phrases **In this wilderness they will finish** and **there they will die** mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [In this wilderness they will end their lives and die]

Yahweh is using **they will finish** as a common expression of his culture to mean “they will die.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they will end their lives] or [they will experience death]

36.note: Here, the pronoun **him** could refer to: (1) Moses. Alternate translation: [against Moses] (2) Yahweh. Alternate translation: [against Yahweh]

Here, the author is speaking as if words were actually something that could be **brought out**, like items that can be carried. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the similar clause in chapter 13:32. Alternate translation: [by giving a bad report]

37.note: It might seem that the expression **the men bringing out an evil bad report of the land** contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [and those men died]

If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [also they died] or [they died]

Here, the author is speaking as if words were actually something that could be brought out, like items that can be carried. See how you translated the similar clause in verse 36. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [giving an evil bad report of]

The implication is that Yahweh sent the **plague** to punish these men. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [to the face of Yahweh in the plague that he sent]

The author is not referring to a specific **plague**. He means an unspecified plague. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [in a plague]
Here, **to the face of** represents being in front of someone. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [before]

38.q: חָיוּ֙ מִן־הָ⁠אֲנָשִׁ֣ים הָ⁠הֵ֔ם הַֽ⁠הֹלְכִ֖ים לָ⁠ת֥וּר אֶת־הָ⁠אָֽרֶץ
38.note: The author is using **from those men** as a common expression of his culture to mean “among those men” or “out of those men.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [lived. They were the only ones who lived among those men, the ones having gone to explore the land]

39.note: Moses is using the term **these words** to represent what Yahweh said by using words. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [what Yahweh had declared]

40.note: The implication is that the Israelites are preparing to leave. In verse 44, the text shows that they actually started marching up to fight. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and prepared to go up] or [and got ready to go up]

In keeping with what is usual for his language and culture, the author is marking travel for change in elevation. If this expression contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [and went]

Here, the author is speaking as if a hill were a person with a **head**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to the heights of the hill country] or [to the top of the hill country]
By **us**, the people mean to include themselves but not Moses to whom they are speaking, so use the exclusive form of that word if your language marks that distinction.

The Israelites are using the term **Behold us** to focus their listeners’ attention on what they are about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Listen to us]

40.q: וְ⁠עָלִ֛ינוּ אֶל־הַ⁠מָּק֛וֹם אֲשֶׁר־אָמַ֥ר יְהוָ֖ה כִּ֥י חָטָֽאנוּ
40.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [We sinned. So, now we will go up to the place that Yahweh said]

In keeping with what is usual for his language and culture, the author is marking travel for change in elevation. If this expression contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [And we will go]

41.q: לָ֥⁠מָּה זֶּ֛ה אַתֶּ֥ם עֹבְרִ֖ים אֶת־פִּ֣י יְהוָ֑ה
41.note: Moses is using the question form to rebuke the Israelites. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Do not pass over the mouth of Yahweh!]

It might seem that the expression **is this** contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [Why are you passing over]

Here, Moses is speaking of disobedience as if it were physically **passing over** God’s command. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [are you transgressing]
Here, **the mouth of Yahweh** represents what Yahweh said by using words. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh’s command]
The pronoun **it** refers to their plan to go up to the high hill country. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And your plan]

42.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Yahweh is not in your midst, so you shall not go up]

In keeping with what is usual for his language and culture, Moses is marking travel for change in elevation. If this expression **go up** contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [You shall not go]

Here, Moses is speaking of **Yahweh** as if he were physically present among the Israelites. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh is not with you] or [Yahweh will not help you]

The expression **shall not be struck** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and your enemies shall not strike you to their face]

The words translated as **and** introduce what will happen if they do not go up. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a result of what came before. Alternate translation: [and that way you shall not be struck]

The implication is that the Israelites will be defeated in battle by their enemies. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. See the discussion of the term “struck” in the Introduction to Numbers. Alternate translation: [and you shall not be defeated]

Here, **to the face of** represents being in front of your enemies. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [before your enemies]

43.note: Here the word **For** introduces not a reason but an explanation. Alternate translation: [More specifically,]

Here, **the Amalekite** and **the Canaanite** represent Amalekites and Canaanites in general, not specific individuals. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use expressions that would be more natural in your language. See how you translated the similar forms in verse 25. Alternate translation: [the Amalekites and the Canaanites]
Here, **to your face** represents being in front of you. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in front of you]

Moses is using **fall by the sword** as a common expression of his culture to mean “die in battle.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the similar words in verse 3. Alternate translation: [and you will die in battle]

43.q: כִּֽי־עַל־כֵּ֤ן שַׁבְתֶּם֙ מֵ⁠אַחֲרֵ֣י יְהוָ֔ה וְ⁠לֹא־יִהְיֶ֥ה יְהוָ֖ה עִמָּ⁠כֶֽם
43.note: Here, the phrase **for upon this** introduces a reason, which is **you returned from after Yahweh**. This clause could be the reason: (1) why the Israelites will fall by the sword. Alternate translation: [since you returned from after Yahweh. And Yahweh will not be with you] (2) why **Yahweh will not be with** them. Alternate translation: [and because you returned from after Yahweh, Yahweh will not be with you]

Here, Moses is speaking as if the Israelites had literally been walking behind Yahweh but then **returned from after** him. He means that they stopped living in the manner in which Yahweh wants people to live. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you stopped following Yahweh] or [you did not do what Yahweh said]

44.note: The implication is that the Israelites were deliberately disobeying Moses and Yahweh by going up to the hill country. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [And they disobeyed Moses and went up]

In keeping with what is usual for his language and culture, the author is marking travel for change in elevation in **to go up**. If this expression contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [to go]

Here, the author is speaking of the hill country as if it had a **head**, meaning its highest point or peak. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated this phrase in verse 40. Alternate translation: [to the heights of the hill country] or [to the top of the hill country]

44.q: וַ⁠אֲר֤וֹן בְּרִית־יְהוָה֙ וּ⁠מֹשֶׁ֔ה לֹא־מָ֖שׁוּ מִ⁠קֶּ֥רֶב הַֽ⁠מַּחֲנֶֽה
44.note: The author is speaking of **the box of the covenant of Yahweh** as if it were a living thing that could depart or stay. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [but no one carried the box of the covenant of Yahweh from the midst of the camp, and Moses also did not depart from the midst of the camp] or [but the box of the covenant of Yahweh and Moses stayed in the midst of the camp]

45.note: Here, **the Amalekite** and **the Canaanite** represent Amalekites and Canaanites in general, not specific individuals. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use expressions that would be more natural in your language. See how you translated the similar forms in verse 25. Alternate translation: [And the Amalekites and the Canaanites, the ones dwelling]

The expression **came down** marks a change in elevation that was usual for the author to express in his language and culture. If this expression contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [came] or [arrived]

The implication is that the Amalekites and Canaanites defeated the Israelites in battle and killed many of them. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. See the discussion of the term “struck” in the Introduction to Numbers. Alternate translation: [And they overpowered them] or [And they won the battle with them]

Here, the author is speaking of defeating the Israelites as if they were objects that they could **beat … to pieces**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and pursued the scattered Israelite soldiers]
The word **Hormah** is the name of a city. It was located south of Beersheba and may be modern-day Tel Masos.

It is very unusual for a name to have the word **the** with it in this language. The use of **the** here may imply that the author intended his readers to think about the meaning of the name **Hormah**, which comes from a word that means “to devote to destruction.” You could consider including this information in a footnote if it would be helpful to your readers.
